entities.summary: José Clemente Orozco was a Mexican caricaturist and painter, who specialized in political murals that established the Mexican Mural Renaissance together with murals by Diego Rivera, David Alfaro Siqueiros, and others. Orozco was the most complex of the Mexican muralists, fond of the theme of human suffering, but less realistic and more fascinated by machines than Rivera. Mostly influenced by Symbolism, he was also a genre painter and lithographer. Between 1922 and 1948, Orozco painted murals in Mexico City; Orizaba; Claremont, California; New York City; Hanover, New Hampshire; Guadalajara, Jalisco; and Jiquilpan, Michoacán.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: As a leading figure of the Mexican Mural Renaissance, Orozco's works had a significant regional impact on Mexican art and culture, influencing generations of artists and shaping the country's identity. His murals also contributed to the development of socialist realism in Mexico.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Orozco's murals played a significant role in shaping Mexico's cultural identity and contributing to the country's post-revolutionary artistic movement. His work had a lasting impact on Mexican art, influencing generations of artists and cementing his place as one of the most important figures of the Mexican Mural Renaissance.
